title: Health insurance — self-employed health insurance deduction
summary: You can typically deduct 100% of premiums for yourself, spouse, and dependents — but only against business income, not below zero.
detailsHtml:
The mechanics

The Self-Employed Health Insurance Deduction (SEHID) is an above-the-line deduction (Schedule 1) for premiums on medical, dental, and qualifying long-term care insurance. It reduces your AGI directly, but only up to your net self-employment income. It does NOT reduce your self-employment tax — only income tax.

ACA marketplace strategy

If your business income is variable, you may qualify for ACA subsidies (Premium Tax Credits) in lower-income years. Many self-employed people structure income across years (accelerating expenses, deferring revenue) to qualify for subsidies in transition years.

The 400% FPL cliff returned in 2026. Congress allowed the enhanced premium tax credits (ARPA/IRA-era) to expire December 31, 2025. For 2026, households with income exceeding 400% of the federal poverty line — about $62,600 (single), $84,600 (couple), or $128,600 (family of four) — are ineligible for any premium tax credit, often resulting in premium increases of $5K–$20K per year. Even one dollar over the threshold triggers full subsidy loss. Pre-tax retirement contributions, HSA contributions, and Roth withdrawals (which don't count toward MAGI) are the standard tools for keeping income below the cliff.
HDHP / HSA combination: Self-employed people can deduct HSA contributions on Schedule 1 (also above the line), independent of the SEHID. Combined, the contractor with an HDHP and an HSA gets premiums deducted plus contributions deducted plus tax-free growth — among the most tax-efficient structures available.
